questions.q: Why don't NFRs typically surface the same way functional requirements do during normal requirements-gathering?
options: Because NFRs are always documented in a separate legal contract that business stakeholders never see
Because most stakeholders think in terms of outcomes rather than named requirement categories, so eliciting NFRs requires an active, structured task the architect has to drive
Because functional requirements are always more important than NFRs
Because Salesforce automatically generates NFRs from the object model
questions.explain: Stakeholders naturally describe functional processes they already understand, but rarely connect an outcome like 'our busiest week can't go down' to a named NFR category — eliciting that connection is active work the architect has to drive deliberately.

questions.q: Why is asking "What happened the last time this process went down, and what did it cost?" more effective than asking "What are your nonfunctional requirements?"
options: Because it's a trick question designed to confuse the stakeholder
Because stakeholders are legally required to answer cost-related questions truthfully
Because it only works for security NFRs, not availability
Because it's concrete and tied to a scenario the stakeholder already understands, which translates directly into an availability/reliability NFR without requiring them to know the terminology
questions.explain: A generic 'what are your NFRs' question gets a blank stare from most stakeholders. A concrete, scenario-based question lets them answer from lived experience, and the architect translates that answer into a specific NFR category — here, availability and reliability.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend requesting existing SLAs, contracts, and policies as an elicitation technique?
options: Because a significant share of real NFRs already exist in writing before the project starts, and the architect's job is to find and translate them, not invent new requirements from scratch
Because SLAs are purely legal documents with no bearing on system design
Because SLAs always override every other NFR category automatically
Because contracts are the only valid source of performance requirements
questions.explain: Customer-facing SLAs, security policies, retention schedules, and regulatory obligations the organization has already committed to are real NFRs waiting to be discovered — often surfacing more requirements than a full round of stakeholder interviews.

questions.q: What is the purpose of running this course's six NFR categories as an explicit checklist against a system being designed?
options: To guarantee every category gets an equally strict target regardless of context
To replace the need for any stakeholder interviews
To force a deliberate decision for each category — even deciding a category barely matters here is a real, explicit decision, rather than a silent, undiscovered gap
To automatically generate governor-limit values for the org
questions.explain: The value of a checklist is forcing an explicit yes/no/doesn't-matter-much decision for each category, so that an absence of a stated NFR reflects a deliberate judgment rather than simply never having been asked about.

questions.q: Why are scenario walkthroughs (e.g., "50,000 cases arrive in six hours after a product recall") especially good at surfacing certain NFRs?
options: Because they only apply to security requirements
Because unusual situations like load spikes are exactly the kind stakeholders wouldn't think to mention in the abstract, even though they're where an NFR gap will be most damaging
Because they eliminate the need to translate vague answers into testable requirements
Because they are required by Salesforce's compliance program before go-live
questions.explain: Scenario walkthroughs surface requirements tied to unusual, high-stakes situations that rarely come up in day-to-day operation, and therefore rarely get mentioned unprompted — even though an NFR gap in exactly that scenario tends to be the most damaging.
